utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Morrison being away due to an urgent personal matter. Before we begin today, I have a couple of housekeeping matters to deal with. First is related to witness Slavko Kralj's Rule 92 ter statement. I meant to raise it when his evidence was concluded, but I simply forgot. The Chamber admitted as Exhibit D3245 a transcript of Kralj's testimony in the Popovic case. However, the Chamber notes that D3245 appears to be the public redacted version of the transcript. Therefore the Chamber wishes to know if there was any particular reason why the accused only tendered the public redacted version instead of tendering both under seal and public redacted versions of transcript, which I think had been the practice in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm remembering back to this one. I was the one that actually reviewed this, and I believe that I determined that what was under seal wasn't relevant to the testimony. So to make it easier, I didn't do a separate version, but if you'd like one we can file it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it to you, Mr. Robinson. For the next matter, could the Chamber move briefly into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless there's another matter to deal with, we'll bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you hear me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, only I have forgotten my glasses in an office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. They will be brought in shortly. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Simic, I must draw your attention to a particular Rule that we have here at the International Tribunal. That is Rule 90(E) of Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you, as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you and to keep reminding myself that we should speak slowly, and it is particularly important that we make a pause between questions and answers so that everything can be interpreted. Mr. Simic, have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D7721 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the screen in front of you. Do you see that statement of yours in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please wait a bit before you start your answer so that everything can be interpreted. Does this statement accurately reflect what you told my Defence team, or is there something that perhaps needs to be corrected?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, I think that this statement reflects everything that I have to say regarding this case to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today as the ones put to you before, would your answers essentially be the same?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Essentially they would be the same, only I could provide some more details if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I tender this statement in evidence, and I believe that there is a document also, but I would leave that to Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're offering one associated exhibit. We ask that it be added to our 65 ter list as the witness hadn't been interviewed at the time that list was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. No, no objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit the statement as well as the associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. The statement will be Exhibit D3398, and 65 ter number 00599 will be Exhibit D3399.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to read Mr. Simic's statement summary in English. [In English] Ljubisav Simic was born on 8th of August, 1953, in Podravanje, Srebrenica municipality. He is a permanent resident of Bratunac and was a member of the SDS from 1990 to 2002 with various positions including president, deputy in the Assembly, and assemblyman. The formation of the SDA and the HDZ in BH left Serbian people very afraid. The subsequent formation of the SDS relaxed the situation. The formation of three representative ethnic parties led to greater co-operation between the ethnic parties and communities. All forums were public and attended by both Serbs and Muslims. At one SDA forum, a speaker made threats of violence and received an ovation from the Muslims present. In response, Muhamed Filipovic, who attended, criticised the speaker and those who supported it. The local SDS organised similar forums at which one-third of participating persons were Muslims. Some vehicles and passengers were injured when returning from SDS central forums while passing through Muslim areas. Muslim extremists came to Kravica to provoke a bigger incident. Although shooting was involved, bloodshed was avoided thanks to quick intervention by authorities and respectable hosts. After the municipality elections, the SDS and SDA became partners in power through agreement without any major problems until it came to bigger political questions at the BH and Federal Republic of Yugoslavia level. The biggest questions gave birth to the extremist orientation of mind in one part of the population. The Muslims were against the JNA and sent policemen and soldiers to be trained in Croatia. Many of them fought against the Serbs in Croatia. The first major incidents started in Bratunac. Attacks on Serbian representatives of government started in opposition to the JNA unit. The Muslims led by SDA leadership threatened violence at the municipality building. Muslims remained after this event and provoked subsequent incidents and ethnic clashes. Communication between the ethnic groups dropped to a minimum and total distrust existed between groups. Many families started to leave Bratunac, especially the Serbs who felt under threat. Both sides collected massive amount of arms. Nijaz Dubicic and Miroslav Deronjic attempted to organise peaceful resolution to the situation by holding an intellectual forum. Some Muslims attempted to stop the meeting. It was agreed that Ljubisav Simic and Nijaz Dubicic talk to both peoples and defuse tensions on the ground. They were badly received. The SDS and SDA agreed to divide the municipality and police into Serbian and Muslim parts. However, the paramilitary units arrived in Bratunac before the process was finished. No one knew who invited them. Security was worsened in Bratunac and Srebrenica when a unit of volunteers was ambushed and killed by a group of Muslims between Srebrenica and Potocari. A larger unit of volunteers prepared to come to Bratunac against the wishes of Ljubisav Simic and others. Their arrival caused immediate problems because local authorities tried to send them away, which turned the public against the civilian authorities and police as well. Other Serbs fleeing Srebrenica came to Bratunac, while others left Bratunac. No agreements were possible with the Muslims after they killed Goran Zekic, a respected judge, and destroyed villages in Srebrenica. As both sides attempted to leave Bratunac in large numbers, Ljubisav Simic and the Crisis Staff issued the decision that permits were required to leave. The leadership wanted a peaceful resolution of the war. However, Naser Oric, from neighbouring Srebrenica, made it clear that Muslims did not want to negotiate. The Muslim population asked to leave Bratunac for their safety. A unit of volunteers singled out some men and took them to Vuk Karadzic primary school. The volunteers maltreated, beat, and killed some of the Muslims. Miroslav Deronjic tried to engage other people to threaten the volunteers to stop but no one dared oppose them. Ljubisav Simic and the Crisis Staff wanted to evacuate the Muslims but knew they would be attacked when the volunteers found out. Risking their personal safety, the Muslims were transferred to Pale by them. Most volunteers then left after being told by authorities that those who did not want to place themselves under the army's command were to leave Bratunac or face arrest and expulsion. Muslims of Srebrenica and Bratunac joined forces and systematically attacked Serbian villages. Many Serbians were killed. Bratunac became surrounded by Muslim forces on all sides except Serbia's direction. No one from Bratunac intended to kill the Muslims. The paramilitary units caused most of the problems. Nobody could control them and everybody was afraid of them. Although Srebrenica was declared a demilitarised zone in 1993, the Muslims remained armed and continued killing. They prepared a large-scale operation to gain control over the area. In July 1995, Srebrenica was defeated militarily. Ljubisav Simic and Srbislav Davidovic joined the Muslim representatives who had asked for transport from Srebrenica and helped them evacuate people to Kladanj. Some buses with Muslims came to Bratunac shortly after and nobody knew who sent them. Ljubisav Simic went to the SDS office to organise security for the Muslims. An evacuation was organised for them and the buses left Bratunac to Potocari. The Muslim population was never forced to move. They asked themselves to be evacuated. President Karadzic never issued any orders that would be fatal to Muslims and ordered all Muslim civilians, wounded and prisoners be treated humanely. He came personally to Bratunac in an attempt to persuade people to allow food convoys to go to Srebrenica and fully supported rule of law. And that would be summary, and at that moment I don't have questions for Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Simic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement, in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just a possible correction for Mr. Karadzic. I don't know if he misspoke at line 9 -- page 9, line 5, where he said: "The evacuation was ordered for them and the buses left Bratunac to Potocari." This is after the prisoners had been brought to Bratunac. I don't know if he meant to say that. I don't believe it's in the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Which line would be, sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be from Potocari to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Or Kladanj or somewhere is what I assume he meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Kladanj -- line 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think it is -- since it is not evidence, but I think it is to -- in the statement said that services have been ordered to facilitate people to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From where to where? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think it concerns Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From Potocari.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I suppose so. We may ask witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is your sixth time testifying?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Third time here at the Tribunal. I gave testimony in Sarajevo I think on four occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm aware of three in the state court. So then that would be your seventh time testifying. Right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Possibly. I'm not good at numbers, and if you have better records, I accept that because I'm not keeping any records. I only know that I testified in many cases in Sarajevo and this is the third time that I'm appearing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And always as a Defence witness; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I've always been called by the Defence, and I responded to their summons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you always told the truth when you testified in court before; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I always spoke about what I knew and what I saw. I never entered into the reign of anything that was said or done by somebody else. What I'm going to speak about today is limited only to what I myself have seen or learned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, please answer my question. You always told the truth in your prior testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What do you mean you think so? You think you might have not told the truth, you might have lied at some point? Or have you always told the truth to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I believe that I always spoke the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many times did you meet with Radovan Karadzic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't think many times, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, which ones do you remember? Just briefly. You know, "I met with him on this date. I met with him on that date. I met with him here, met with him there."

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I do remember that on one occasion I visited him in his office in order to accelerate the development of a neighbourhood in Bratunac that was being financed by the Norwegian people's relief or an NGO at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. Just a second. I don't want to cut you off but listen to my question carefully. I didn't ask you why you met with him or what you talked about. I just want to know when and where you met with him. Okay? And if it becomes important to talk about what you were meeting for, what the purpose was, we'll get into that. So when and where did you meet with Karadzic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I remember meeting him for the first time in Zvornik where General Mladic was present as well. It was 1992, and I think that during that same year the president came to Bratunac on account of certain difficulties we were experiencing with the passage of humanitarian aid into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on. I want to move right to 1995 and talk about the Hotel Fontana meeting you attended and the early morning meeting at the brigade that you attended before that. First let's talk about the meeting at the Bratunac Brigade at 8.00 a.m. on 12 July. You remember going to that meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General Mladic was there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Some other army officers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No other officers were present there. There were a few soldiers present who I believe to have been his personal security or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Srbislav Davidovic was there and Aleksandar Tesic was there.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Aleksandar Tesic and Srbislav Davidovic, the president of the Executive Board, who informed me on the eve of that meeting that he and I had been called to report to Mladic's office in the brigade's HQ in Bratunac, and we went together --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, okay --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Davidovic and I went together, and Aco may have come a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered the question who was there. Now I want to read you a bit of your testimony from the Bozic case in the state court from 2008. This is 65 ter 24918 at e-court page 81. Question -- this is about that meeting. "Q. Was any discussion made at that meeting about transport for Muslims from Srebrenica and the need to get as many trucks as possible and buses? Answer from you: "No." "Q. You see I -- "A. You mean at the command. No, no, not a single word of mention. Who could mention it, given that we did not know what proposal of the Srebrenica people would be, Srebrenica people who would come to the meeting." You stand by that truthful testimony; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I can talk about it a million times and I will never add anything to it. It's an easy conversation to remember. It was short and I remember it fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. So: "No, no, not a single word of mention." Let's look at what Aleksandar Tesic, another Karadzic Defence witness, said about this same meeting in this court. This is in his Defence statement, D03118, at paragraphs 34 to 35. In paragraph 34 he says that you were present along with some other army officers and that General Mladic asked him: "What are we going to do with all these people?" In paragraph 35, Aleksandar Tesic's testimony states that General Mladic said: "Buses and trucks must be mobilised immediately to transport about 20.000 residents today or tomorrow." And then he says how as part of the MOD he went to arrange that and then sent out call-up paper for buses. So it's not true what you said in your state court testimony and what you just testified here that there was no mention at the 8.00 a.m. meeting about transporting the population.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I stand by my previous evidence now, and I will repeat. I told you that I can repeat this countless times. The conversation unfolded as I depicted it. Now, whether Tesic stayed behind after I and the President of the Executive Board left, because we were there for a brief period of time only, perhaps Tesic heard it and he's convinced of it. But, however, in my presence and in the presence of Srbislav Davidovic, no mention was made of trucks or transport. Let me repeat again. The only sentence that General Mladic said as far as I heard it was: "Srebrenica has fallen. What are we going to do next?" Since Davidovic and I were seated and I was closer to him, I was looking at him and realised that he was expecting me to answer the question of how we were going to protect the civilian population and ensure security in the Srebrenica area in general. I realised that he was expecting to hear my opinion of whether the Bratunac police, the army, or whoever was supposed to be dealing with these issues was capable of seeing this through. I wanted to be resolute in what I was saying, that as for the security of the civilian population now after the defeat, that in view of the events that had been unfolding previously, it was not possible to have any confidence in the local structures and that ways and means of ensuring the security of the civilian population had to be sought at higher levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that's an interesting answer because in Mr. Tesic's statement, it is directly when General Mladic asks that question which you've just said is when you were there, the discussion about the need to get buses and trucks to remove the population takes place. So it was while you were present according to Mr. Tesic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: What I've said and what I'm going to say, I can take the lie detector if you want and repeat these things. Did Tesic remain there for a longer period of time after we left, I don't know. The only thing I know that the last sentence that I heard him say after I said what I've just told you, that a meeting would be held at Fontana at 10.00 a.m., that the meeting would be attended by the representatives of the military and civilian authorities together with representatives of the DutchBat, and that we would hear them out at that meeting, what their view was, and that was all that I heard at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't want to cut you off but that's in your statement and you stand by it. I understand. So you have no problem coming to my office sometime and taking a lie detector test and having us question you about what happened in Srebrenica and what you knew and what you did? Is that a serious offer from you? We might be able to arrange that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I've just told you so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P02996.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a document the Trial Chamber has seen before. It will come up on your screen, sir. I don't want to spend a lot of time on it. P02996. And again, you said there was no mention at this meeting of buses and trucks because before 10.00 a.m., nobody knew what the Muslim population in Potocari representatives would suggest. This is a dispatch from centre chief Dragomir Vasic. It's a report up his chain. If you look at point 2, it discusses that a meeting was held at Bratunac at the brigade command at 8.00. The same time you said you were at the Bratunac Brigade command that day. And in point 5, it says a meeting will begin or is beginning or something to convey that a meeting will start at 10.00 at the Hotel Fontana at which an agreement will be reached on the evacuation of the civilian population. And then it says a hundred trailer trucks have been provided for transport. So apparently you were the only person at this meeting and of these high officials in Bratunac who had no clue that before the 10.00 a.m. Fontana meeting, it was already decided to get trucks and buses to remove the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes. Before you answer. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I object to that question because it's misleading, because the Prosecution's own witness, Srbislav Davidovic testified at page 24429 of the trial transcript that he also had no knowledge of these -- of these arrangements to evacuate. So for Mr. Nicholls to suggest that Mr. Simic is the only one in the world who didn't have this knowledge, I think is misleading given the evidence that we've heard elicited from their own witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll rephrase that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I remember there was a translation issue in particular with respect to the tense. So I was wondering whether we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- ask the CLSS to take up this issue -- do you remember, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if it has been. I -- taken up by CLSS, but I would agree that they do it. I had a language assistant check the document and the language assistant told me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So for the purpose of today's testimony, could you ask the witness to read out paragraph 2 and paragraph 5 and proceed with your question, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Simic, could you please read out paragraph 2 of the Vasic report and then paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I've looked at it and I've realised what your problem is. Your problem is in understanding the term "meeting."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, before you answer the question, could you kindly read out paragraph 2 and paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. "At 800 hours at the HQ of the Bratunac Brigade, a meeting was held with Generals Mladic and Krstic where tasks were assigned to all participants." Under 5: "At 1000 hours, a meeting will begin with representatives of UNPROFOR and International Red Cross as well as the Muslim representative from Srebrenica where an agreement or a deal will be reached on the evacuation of all the civilian population from Potocari to Kladanj so that they would there have more problems" -- well, I don't get this, but I've read it. Now, let me finish off what I've just started. You obviously seem to understand this to mean that we met, all of us met there, whereas I only saw General Krstic later. And I can repeat this at the lie detector. And obviously, Davidovic and I arrived there first and we heard what I told you that we heard, and then Mladic requested that we go home and get ready for the 10.00 meeting. We did so. We were told that we would hear what their representatives think about this and certain conclusions would be reached there. Now, perhaps in that same office there were meetings between Mladic and other people, because he'd finished with us and he told us that we were free to go. Now, who stayed behind or who arrived there later is something I don't know. And I cannot speak for others. I am sure about Tesic. I'm sure that he was there. Did he arrive a bit later, what happened, I don't know. I know that I arrived there together with Davidovic, we had a cup of coffee, and I heard that one sentence that I repeated and I said what I've just told you that I said. I left then. I expected Miroslav to be there, and I expected it to be just an ordinary meeting. However, it wasn't -- it didn't look like at a meeting at all. There was no discussion. There was no talking about anything. There was just this exchange that I told you about. There was Vasic. There was Krstic there. However, at the time that I was there, they weren't there, absolutely. There were only the people that I told you were there. There was Davidovic, Tesic who may have arrived later, I don't know if he stayed behind, and the two of us left and that's absolutely correct. Now, what happened next, how long this meeting took and who was there is something that I don't know. I went straight home.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 4, page 18, the witness said, "I saw General Krstic later only in Fontana," and this "only in Fontana" is not in the transcript. And I do believe that his Excellency Mr. Kwon expected the last sentence to be read out as well because that's where the translation problem lies. The last sentence just before paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that this English translation is the one that has been revised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, we'll get to the Hotel Fontana meeting, but your -- your testimony and what we heard from Mr. Karadzic in his summary that the Muslim population that was gathered in Potocari left voluntarily; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I was present at the meeting, and I heard the representative of the Muslim civilian population say that they wanted to be urgently evacuated, and should nothing be organised for them, then they would be heading from Bratunac to Tuzla as best they can, which would be complete chaos. Now, if you want me to talk about their proposals at the meeting, I can tell you that they sought evacuation to be arranged for them. They asked for transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. So now let's now do it as a yes or no. Is it your position that the Muslim population left Potocari voluntarily; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see up there, nobody forced anyone to board a bus. During my presence there --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: -- I did not see anyone being forced or coerced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. Tell me if you can't answer this question yes or no. Is your position that the Muslim population left Potocari voluntarily? Is that your position, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, I did say that they wanted to leave Srebrenica voluntarily on the transport that was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So that's a yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. That means that the women and children could come back if they wanted to; right? There wouldn't have been any problem with women coming back to Potocari or Srebrenica if they so chose; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know when. After they'd gone to Kladanj, come back from where? They were in Potocari. The entire population was in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Say -- say they got on the buses, they came to Bratunac where they stopped and some of those women said, You know what, I've changed my mind, I want to go back to Potocari. That wouldn't have been a problem, right, with you in the leadership in Bratunac or the army? You wouldn't force them not to return to their homes; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Nobody forced them on the buses either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're not answering -- you're not --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: As for what their disposition or mood was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question was: Would there have been any problem, from your experience as being at the Hotel Fontana meeting, as being president of the Municipal Board, would there have been any problem if women in the next few days changed their mind and said they wanted go back to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: In my mind, it would not have been a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And if women had gotten lost in the woods, the VRS would have helped them, do you think? Right? Civilians walking around in the woods who got lost.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I cannot speak on behalf the army. I was not a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I am not placed or in a position to speak about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P03994, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this might come as a revelation to you, then, what the army's position was. General Krstic who was at the meeting with you. This is a Drina Corps command report from the 17th of July, 1995. So that's four days after the enclave has been cleansed. It's a regular combat report to the Main Staff of the VRS. I'd like you to look at number 3 in your language. The territorial situation in the zone of responsibility. And if you look down you'll see: In the last three days following the transportation of the civilian population from the former Srebrenica enclave to Kladanj, there have been increasing instances of women who have allegedly got lost coming back towards us from Kladanj and arriving at our forward line of defence. After being warned by our soldiers they try to run away. Yesterday, two women arrived from Kladanj direction at the first VLPBR's point of defence in the Luka sector, and as they refused to surrender and began to run away towards Kladanj, they were fired on and died as a result. So after this voluntary departure of the Muslim women from Kladanj, those women who got lost in the woods and started walking back towards the enclave were killed by Krstic's troops. Now, does that sound to you like there was any voluntariness in their ability to move or do what they wanted to? The man you were in the meeting with is shooting -- his troops are shooting women in the woods who get lost.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know why I should be called upon to explain or account for things happening in a war zone which is in the jurisdiction of the army. These things can be interpreted in a number of ways. I could interpret them in one way, but I don't want to draw any conclusions, and on the basis of this one instance where there were two straying women who came upon a group of soldiers. They started running away, and they shot them. I could interpret this in one way, but it can be interpreted in a number of ways. And I'm really -- I really regret that this happened. I regret that this case happened and that there was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Well, the reason is that it's relevant to call upon you to ask this is because you were part of the group at the third Hotel Fontana meeting. You were there as the highest representative of Bratunac from the municipality, along with Deronjic, and you were assuring these people that their wishes would be respected and that they would be safe. So I think it is relevant to call upon you when those very same people you made those promises to get lost in the woods and they're shot by the subordinates of another man who was present at the meeting. And as an intelligent man, I think you would be able to look at this document and be able to tell what it says about the voluntariness of these women to move where they wanted to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm going to object to this as being argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's not argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the witness has answered the question, and then without asking another -- asking for any additional information, Mr. Nicholls has just simply made an argument back to the witness on facts that really can be interpreted, as the witness said, in many ways given that women disobeyed an order to surrender. So there's many ways this can be interpreted. The witness gave his answer and now Mr. Nicholls is simply arguing with the witness because he doesn't like the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that's not true, Your Honour. If I can just respond quickly and then I'll move on. I had no problem with the answer. The witness asked why he was being asked about this, as though he had no connection to these events, and in cross-examination, asked and answered is not always an appropriate objection when, and my position would be, the witness is trying to evade answering these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since the witness is not in a position to answer why those women ran away at the time, so I would -- I'm going to advise you to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I will move on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show part of the hotel -- I don't have time to show the whole meeting like I'd like to but I'll show you part of the Hotel Fontana meeting you were present at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have P04201. That's the trial video. Part 2 I'm going to play from 5:30 to 7 minutes, 12 seconds. In the book, P04202, this meeting is at English e-court 245 to 250, and Serbian 344 to 349.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We stopped at 7:22, a little bit farther than I said. Could we now jump to 12 minutes, 52 seconds, please, Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's you smoking a cigarette, sitting at Mladic's right hand; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can keep playing a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's Mr. Davidovic next to you. We stopped --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- at 13:07. Now, you were there at this meeting with Miroslav Deronjic and we also saw Vasic from the police; correct? You need to answer yes --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we also saw General Krstic, among others.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen him yet. Maybe I didn't watch carefully enough, but it doesn't matter. I'm certain that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. You're not in that screen shot. And across from you is a man we saw from the Muslim people in Potocari, Ibro Nuhanovic. You remember him; right? We just -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You shook his hand?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. And later we sat down and had a drink after the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So you shake his hand, you have a drink. This is the meeting where it's decided that the Muslim population will be allowed to go wherever it wants to go or stay and enjoy their freedom of movement. Can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you. Just a second. I'm not sure -- could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just remark that this translation isn't right either, because General Mladic said that one representative should be with their people. This part, their people, was not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I would like you to put in writing if you would like to request a revised transcript. Let's continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, in your state court testimony in the Bozic case in 2008 - that's 65 ter 2918, e-court page 41 for Mr. Robinson - you testified how you did not see the Muslim representatives in Potocari when you went there. You didn't see this man whose hand you shook and who you had a drink with; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you know, don't you, that that man whose hand you shook, who you sat across from in the meeting, was separated in Potocari, held overnight in your town Bratunac, and then murdered on 16 July? You know that, don't you, as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I know that today, but I had no idea at the time. Miroslav brought some kind of document according to which everything finished well, and it was signed, but at the time I didn't really look into that. It wasn't for me to do so. And that man must have been one who was a member of a commission of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you say it wasn't for you to look into it or do so, but you're taking part in this meeting at the Hotel Fontana that is filmed, we say, for pure propaganda purposes. The fact that this man, you shook his hand, you're at the meeting where he's guaranteed his safety, he ends up dead four days later, doesn't that show that that entire meeting was pure theatre for the cameras? When the people who are at the meeting on the other side are murdered. That man at least.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: That's not a question for me. I don't think so. I still don't think that's why the meeting was called. I disagree with your view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why is it not a question for you when you are president of the Municipal Board. You are sitting there at Mladic's right hand. You are there representing Bratunac and the civilian authorities in Bratunac along with Srbislav Davidovic and Miroslav Deronjic. You are part of the group guaranteeing these people their safety. Then they're brought to your town and held overnight and then they're killed. Why do you think that's not a problem for you as municipal president?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I cannot guarantee anybody's safety. Only the army or the police could do so. I was not called upon to guarantee anything to anybody but only to hear what would be agreed upon. And General Mladic at that meeting proposed and required us to work as one team, both at Fontana and at Potocari, and that we should register our problems on the ground and request them for help, because the three of us are only three individuals. Our task is to provide food and water for the civilians, because we had learned that the people had slept for two nights in a row in the open and under difficult conditions. It was hot. And we got very specific tasks to help those people and, together with these men, build a team that will register and report about problems. This part that you showed was the informal part of the meeting. It was a free conversation and exchange of views. The man who sat with Mladic, I heard him say -- I heard Mladic say, that is, "There will be no problems. We will escort the buses and see that there are no problems." What could I have done there? What else should I have done?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- let's go on to a topic you talked about, your task providing food, and you talk about that in your statement which you don't need to see at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to comment on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that Mladic said - that's line 6, page 28 - that that man would be taken somewhere in his car, and so he would be transported by car and not by bus. Perhaps we can check with the witness and ask him to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mladic and this man were sitting a couple of tables away and having a drink. I didn't overhear their conversation, but when that man stood up and Mladic was getting ready to leave, I heard him say, "If everything is all right, the way we agreed, if need be you will be taken somewhere," I don't remember where, "in my car." And probably these people were among the first to leave. That's why Davidovic and I didn't meet anyone up there when we arrived. We expected someone to turn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You've fixed the transcript and you're not answering any question from me, so I want to move on. I'm going to read back some of your testimony from the Blagojevic case. You tell me if you still stand by it, if it's still true. This is at 65 ter 24914 at e-court pages 34 to 35. You're talking about the conditions you see when you go to Potocari and about Srebrenica. You remember you met some female students there. You said: "And from talking to my female students, as I told you, I heard that they regretted not having been able to leave Srebrenica much earlier. Life there had been very difficult for some time, and many people wished for a way out of the situation. The number of people there that I realised only then was so great had to leave a very difficult life." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said this in your Mitrovic state court testimony, which is 65 ter 24916, this is at e-court pages 10 -- or 11, excuse me, that you heard that Srebrenica was overpopulated, that the conditions of life and accommodation were terrible, and "that is why I understood that they were sincere when they said that the majority of the people wanted to leave Srebrenica and that would be the request of most of them." That's also true. You stand by that; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And you also testified in your Blagojevic testimony that -- you were asked this question, this is 65 ter 24914, e-court page 47: "Were you aware that in March 1995 that President Karadzic, the top member of the SDS, had ordered the army, the VRS, to make life impossible for the inhabitants of Srebrenica? "A. I was not aware of such an order. I never saw or received such an order from anyone. "Q. Were you aware that this order included an order to restrict the flow of goods to that enclave and make the inhabitants of the enclave dependent on the goodwill of the Serbs? "A. I already said that I never saw such an order, nor did I participate, nor could I have participated in such an action." And that's true, isn't it? You never knew about such an order or directive; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: That is my statement, too. I don't know about such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Let me tell what you said about your knowledge of convoys in the Blagojevic case. This is, again, 24914, e-court page 48. "Q. Were you aware that the humanitarian convoys to the enclave were slowly cut off and restricted at an ever increasing rate? "A. I don't know. I had no information as to who was sending the convoy nor did I know how much was needed up there to distribute it to everyone. So I don't know why you're asking me this." And further down, that's at e-court pages 49 to 50, you say: "The convoys passed through Bratunac and I saw them passing through the town. Now, as to who was sending them, I knew nothing about that. I couldn't increase the speed or volume or decrease it or do anything about it. I had nothing to do with international humanitarian aid." And further down the same page: "I didn't know what were the needs of the Srebrenica enclave. I didn't know how much aid they needed --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "I didn't know whether what was arriving there was sufficient or insufficient, and I don't know why I should have known this." You stand by that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you started talking about how you brought food to the enclave. That was your task from the meeting. So that's in paragraph 74 of your statement. And that paragraph ends talking about when you went to Potocari. "There I met Davidovic who told me that he had not seen any of those who had been at the meeting. When the first quantities of food arrived, I joined in the distribution." And there's something left out of that part of your statement. I want to read what you said about this food that you took part in distributing in the Blagojevic trial on direct examination from the Defence lawyer. That's at e-court page 15: "The food was a drop in the sea, I must say. I was surprised when I realised what the situation was. I'd never seen anything like it. It was shocking and remains shocking to me to this day." And that's also true, isn't it, that the food you provided was a drop in the sea of what was needed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, given the needs that I could assess with my bare eyes, without the UNHCR aid which was promised, waiting for this aid, but although I didn't see anyone taking -- making video recordings there nor did I see myself in a recording, but the need was certainly much greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: We're talking about five trucks --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me go to that convoy. There's a mistake, we can call it that, in paragraph 85 of your statement, where it says: "A UNHCR convoy got to Potocari in the sunset of 12 July 1992." Now, we can save some time here maybe. Our case is that no UNHCR convoy arrived till 13 July, late, when the population had already been removed. Do you accept that? That's the documentation we have.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Could you please put a specific question very concisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There is a mistake in your statement at paragraph 85. The UNHCR convoy arrived at around sunset on 13 July, not 12 July.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise immediately. I said at the outset that I have a problem with dates. On the day of the evacuation, if that's the 12th, the UNHCR convoy arrived in the evening hours. That's correct. If I made a mistake with the date and I said that I had a problem with numbers so I cannot guarantee with any dates, but I'm sure about the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let -- let me make this very simple. Are you saying the UNHCR convoy arrived on the same day that you attended the Hotel Fontana meeting? Our case and the documents show that it arrived the next day.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the same day. It can't have arrived on the following day. It arrived on the same day in the evening hours. If you will, I'll gladly answer any questions of yours connected to a lie detector. I made a phone call as soon as I was able to see what I would get from Ljubovija --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: -- would not even cover the basic needs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm a bit confused about the date. Are we talking about 1992 or 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 1995, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you have your statement with you? Paragraph 85 refers to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think my friends will stipulate that that's an error and it's meant to say "1995," because this is -- UNHCR is going to Potocari at the time that the buses are leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic. We'll confirm with -- no, no --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We shall confirm with the witness. Do you have your statement with you now, Mr. Simic? It's paragraph 85.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't believe he has it in hard copy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read out --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here the 12th of July, but no matter what it says, I have a memory based on events. After the meeting, in the evening hours, when I was tasked to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Simic --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: -- to provide humanitarian aid --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Simic, this [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So my question is, Mr. Simic, for you, whether it should be 1995, the year itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1995, yes. This is a mistake. I've only noticed now. Yes, it is 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Could I have, very quickly, P04160.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a sitrep from the enclave. It's not in your language so I'll read it to you. And I'll put our case to you which is that all the evidence in our case, from our witnesses, is that no convoy arrived on the 12th but that a convoy arrived on the 13th, the second day of the evacuation, the day after the Hotel Fontana meeting. And this is what this sitrep report says. It's dated 13 July 1995, at 1900 hours, approximately, a little after.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It should come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the exhibit number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 04160. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now number 2 says the - the - UNHCR convoy came in as the last refugees went out. What an expert timing. So our contemporaneous reports show that the convoy arrived too late on the night of the 13th, the second day of the evacuation. Do you accept you made a mistake in your statement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: You know something? You can even quote extraterrestrials. I am sure that it was -- that this is not correct. The convoy arrived on the 12th in the evening hours. Any other stories are unacceptable to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, and your testimony is that when it arrived DutchBat said, We've got so much food, we don't need this. Take it to Bratunac. The UNHCR food convoy.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: When the convoy arrived in the evening -- you want me to paint a bigger picture so it may be more easier for you to understand. I intervened in time. It may have been around 11.00 or 12.00, because I didn't know what I would be able to raise. When I saw that it was insufficient, I remembered to call them too, and not just them but also a team of ours which had been organised during the war for fast interventions. I wanted to involve everybody into the transportation of aid for the people at Potocari. When they arrived in the early evening hours --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, sorry --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: -- the evacuation of that part of the population --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You've answered the question. You stand by it was the 12th at night. Okay, now I want to move on a bit --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. You made that clear. I want to move on now to your movements, your actions over the nights 12th and 13th, the nights everybody describes as chaos in Bratunac, at least the 13th. Now, in your testimony in the Mitrovic case, in 2007, in the state court - that's 65 ter 24916 at e-court page 20 - you talk about how the day after the Hotel Fontana meeting, you arrived at work a bit late and then you went and you saw Davidovic. And you testified about how it was difficult because it had been necessary to mobilise people in the night to -- to provide security to the buses. Right? That's a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I'll accept it for the time being. Let's see how it continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And one thing you said, and this is in your testimony, that when you met Srbislav Davidovic, your testimony states: "The president of the Executive Committee was justifiably scared. He complained and so was I, so we asked to see someone to go out and look for an officer and ask what they were doing to stop it urgently. That is to continue the evacuation as planned rather than having them standing up in the stadium since it was torture. And it posed a permanent danger, and we were afraid of possible incidents." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it's true?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I remember it still. I remember how I felt at the time, and I stand by it. Yes, it was exactly that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you also said in that testimony that it was very hot at that time, even in the morning.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 24618, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While this is coming up, I'll say this is a transcript of a PBS documentary with interviews from January 25, 1996, called "Bosnia's Graves." It's in English, sir. If we could go to page 2. I don't remember if you remember being interviewed by these people. If we can go to page 2, please. And there's a picture of you at the top from the interview. Now, if we go back to page 1. The interviewer says that you said during the interview that no one from Srebrenica was brought to Bratunac. And later on you said: "What can I say? If there was really something going on there and there really were some soldiers dying and were buried there, what can I say. If such things really existed, then it shall be investigated by the military to find out how these things happened." So when you were interviewed six months, approximately, after these events, you told the press that no Muslims were brought to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, where do we see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's on the first page, "the town of Bratunac is the centre of his administration." It's just talking with Mr. Simic. And it says, "the mayor said no one from Srebrenica was brought here," and they refer to Mr. Simic as the mayor in this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was not correct, was it, when you told the international press that no one was brought from Srebrenica to your town?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I have this text in English, and I believe that you are relating the contents of it, and I can only believe you. However, it is very difficult out of context to discuss what the question was and what the answer was. I learned about this the next morning in Milici from the president of the Executive Committee, and after I had talked to an officer whom I had met in town, and after that I went on my way. As for the questions put to me, I cannot give you any more details because it's in a language that I don't understand, and I cannot see what the context is. And if I said something, it might have been construed as wrong or imprecise. I don't remember this, and when I was interviewed, I can say that at the time I was always open to talking to journalists, but as it is, all I can see is my photo there and the rest I cannot understand. I don't remember this particular journalist and this particular interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think this is fair to the witness to put this that way to him, and if you look at that paragraph, when it says, "the mayor said no one from Srebrenica was brought here," look at what was said right before: "We filmed the locked changing rooms under the stand. The walls are riddled with bullet holes." So the "here" that the mayor said that "no, no one from Srebrenica was brought here" may just as well refer or probably even does refer to the rooms underneath the stadium as opposed to whether they were brought to the town of Bratunac. So I think it would be better, if he wants an answer to this question, to have read out to the witness what the reporter is saying as opposed to paraphrasing it in a way that I don't think is the only reasonable way that that could be read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, is Mr. Robinson's point that the stadium is not in the town of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, my point is that the witness never denied that the prisoners were brought to Bratunac, that it appears that he may have simply denied that they were brought to this room underneath the stadium that was riddled with bullet holes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. For me, I still have a problem finding the passage. Where is it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's on the very bottom of page 1 where you see the word "Jane Bennett Powell," and it has a picture of a building and a field, and just to the right of that picture is the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's the same thing, I would say, Your Honour, whether they were brought to the town or to the stadium because the witness testified in the state court that they were brought to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What -- I'm looking at the answer given by the ... I'll leave it to you to continue or to explore further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Shall we take a break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6292, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, 13 July 1995, because you're not good at dates, that's the day after the Hotel Fontana meeting you attended. Let me just read you some more of your testimony in the state court. This is from the Bozic case, 65 ter 24918, e-court page 113. You were asked a question by

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GLUHAJIC
utterances.text: "Does this mean that on 13 July you did not see any buses in Bratunac?" So the day after Hotel Fontana meeting. Your answer: "No. On 13th of July, no. No, no, on 13 July." And that's -- do you stand by that testimony, you didn't see any buses in Bratunac on the day after the Hotel Fontana meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the morning of that day I saw what I testified about, and I was informed by Srbislav Davidovic that there was a convoy. I heard of it, but I didn't go over there to see it and I didn't see it personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: So I believed that this man had no reason to make that up, so I understood that to be a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked, again that same testimony, e-court page 115: "You did not see any buses throughout the night of 13, 14, anywhere?" And your answer was: "No. On the 13th and 14th I was not -- I was not in the town because this was not during my working hours, and at that time I was at my home. "Q. Let's just cover that. What time did you go home on the 13th?" Your answer was: "I cannot tell you with certainty. It was my practice that I would leave office if I did not have additional duties at around 1500." Is that testimony true?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So let me just get the picture clear. 13 July, in Bratunac, you're president of the Municipal Assembly. At about 1500 hours, you go home and don't see anything on the night of the 13th into the 14th; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Between the 13th and the 14th, well, I will have to rely on my memory and you will decide whether it coincides with your question. The evacuation took place on the 12th. I came to the municipality a little bit earlier because the president of the Executive Committee told me that during the previous night --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Stop, stop --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: -- a convoy with men had arrived --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Stop. I don't have much time. I don't want to interrupt you. You're now talking about the morning of the 13th, when you came to work, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: The morning of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, stop. I'm not asking you about the morning of the 13th. I'm asking you about the evening of the 13th, night into the next day the 14th. Do you stand by your testimony that during that time you're at home, you didn't see any buses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I stand by it. I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, on the night of the 13th, the evidence in this case, including from many witnesses on both sides, is that there were buses all over Bratunac holding prisoners and that there were prisoners held in the Vuk Karadzic school and the hangar behind the school and that there were not enough people to guard these prisoners. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: If that is what they saw, that must have been the case. I didn't have an opportunity to witness that or to see anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now just let me be clear. You keep talking about the evacuation on the 12th. Is it your testimony that the evacuation of the people in Potocari was completed on the same day as the Hotel Fontana meeting that you attended?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: No. Some of the population who were on the DutchBat battalion compound were evacuated the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you've testified in the state court that you had access to a uniform and a gun for emergencies. That's at 65 ter 24918 at P64 -- at page 64 and at page 11. Why was it left to old men, young people, to guard all the prisoners? Why were you at home in bed when you're in your 40s and had a uniform and a gun? Why didn't you help guard the prisoners? Are you sure you didn't?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm absolutely sure that I didn't do that. Nobody asked me to do it. The fact that we had uniforms and rifles, that meant that that was for emergency situations when an alert signal would be sounded, and that meant that we should join the nearest unit. That was the purpose of it. Now, in this particular situation, I didn't carry a rifle. There was no need for that. Nobody requested me to do that, and probably that's the reason why they never invited me to join. Obviously there were enough people in Bratunac who were able bodied and people who were in the police, and they guarded them. And this convoy which was returned to Bratunac, I protested with one of the officers that I encountered on my way --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not talking about the officer. We'll talk about that later. Thank you. Now, this is from your Bozic testimony, January 2008, in the state court. 65 ter 24918, P -- page 118. "Q. Did you ever hear that Bosniak prisoners were killed at Vuk Karadzic school regardless of who did it?" This is in 2008. Your answer was: "To tell you the truth, no. Why I don't know, I just didn't. "Q. The most notorious scandal of your town, a piece of modern history including that huge killings as part of its facts, are you seriously saying that you've never been told about it?" Your answer was: "A. No one ever said a single word to me on this incident." So is your honest, truthful testimony that, as of 2008, nobody had told you about the Vuk Karadzic school murders of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I can sincerely tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. You answered. Same -- same case, page 119: It was so secret in the days that followed the killings you never heard a rumour about them. Is that the position? And your answer was: "In the days following we had other tasks and duties pertaining to the organisation of the government in Srebrenica, to protect the town from looting and other affairs of that sort. Therefore, I was not in a position to walk around to observe, to gather any information because I had to attend other tasks." Truthful testimony?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: It is truthful, and I can repeat it in the same manner. Perhaps the reason why I wasn't more vigilant was because I had never expected such things to happen. There was no indication that I observed to that effect. That is why I didn't pay enough attention. Perhaps my mistake was because I believed that everything would go as agreed at the meeting and that no incidents would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Well, in this trial, Branimir Tesic testified that he learned about these killings when the school was vacated and civilian protection entered. That's on 12 March 2013. Aleksandar Tesic testified that over the next days he learnt from Ljupko Ilic of the bodies at the Vuk Karadzic school. That was on 12 March 2013, same day. Milenko Katanic, on cross-examination from Mr. Karadzic, testified that he learned about these killings at the Vuk Karadzic school the day after, on 14 July. So you, the president of the municipality, do not know anything about what's going on in your municipality on the crucial days of 13, 14 July; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Uh-huh. I want to talk about Kravica warehouse executions. Now, you've claimed, and I don't think the Defence will dispute me on this, your claim is that you heard about the Kravica executions on the next day after they had occurred. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And with -- you learned that from Jovan Nikolic; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is from your -- I'll move ahead a bit. Your -- and at that time you knew that Deronjic was civilian commissioner in charge Srebrenica civilians, Muslim civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I've heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you knew it. Are you seriously telling me that you did not know that Miroslav Deronjic was appointed --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Why? Why are you interpreting it in such a way? If I say that I had heard that he had been appoint [indiscernible] Karadzic in charge of civilian affairs, that was correct, but I didn't know what his specific duties were and I never inquired. It was beyond my interest. That was his duty and he knew what he was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. But I can read you back your testimony if you want, but the civilians he was to take care of were Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. This is -- I'm going to quote you now from your testimony in the Mitrovic case in the state court. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel please slow down when reading. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is from your Mitrovic testimony, 65 ter 24916, in e-court at pages 21 to 22, and 22 to 23. Question from Defence counsel and this is talking about when you first discuss hearing about the Kravica warehouse and executions from Jovan Nikolic. "Q. Earlier you mentioned Mr. Deronjic, now deceased. Did you know anything about -- did he know anything about it? Did you have any meetings with him or -- "Witness Simic: No, I did not manage to see him that day at all. He had his tasks and I heard that he had received them from Radovan Karadzic. He was appointed as -- I don't know the exact title, but he was tasked with the security of civilians, so to say, if I may paraphrase, as I cannot say what exactly his duty and his sphere of work were. Since I was busy with what I was doing, I did not manage to meet with him. He probably heard about it later and probably forwarded the information." "Question from Defence counsel Krunic: And did you mention the incident when you were together with Deronjic and you and what did he -- "Witness Simic: Yes. I found out that he had informed Radovan about what had happened." That was truthful testimony, too, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And later on in the Bozic trial, 65 ter 24918, e-court pages 69 to 70, you were asked --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in the Serbian because what Mr. Nicholls quoted previously, we couldn't see this on the current page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It should be the Serbian pages 22. Sorry, Serbian page 30. No -- yes, sorry, first time was right. Serbian page 22 or 23. I'll leave that to Mr. Karadzic's redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to move quickly now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Next page for the English. Give me a minute so that I can see the page. What page was it, Mr. Nicholls? English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: English page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: E-court page 22. It's right in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let me go quickly to 1992, and if we have time we'll come back to 1995 for some other questions I wanted to ask you. You talk in your statement, and it was in your summary about the transfer of Muslim men in 1992 from the stadium to Pale. That's what I'm going to ask you about, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 24913.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While it's coming up, sir, this is a statement you gave on 22nd August 2003 to the RS MUP, and you were informed that if you gave false testimony in this statement that you could be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I want to go to page 5 of the English and page 4 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the part I'm interested in is this, talking about the prisoners who are being tortured and killed in the stadium by the paramilitaries according to you: "The president of the Crisis Staff informed the civilian and military authorities in Pale about the events and asked for a solution to the problems that had been created. I don't know at whose approval -- in any event, it was obtained from Pale. We were given the assignment of transferring the captured men to Pale where the men were supposed to be exchanged." And then you say that this was carried out. That's true, too, isn't it, what you say in your sworn statement to the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Then according to your statement, in paragraph 65, after this takes place, and it was in your summary, the paramilitaries were told by the police to leave and most of them did so; right?
