utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that they were even taken into custody by the police and that they were told that unless they left immediately that they would be arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you could finish your answer, please. The interpreters missed a little bit of it. After arrested. You said the police told them they would be arrested, the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: If they do not place themselves under the command of the local army or the Territorial Defence. I don't know how it was called at the time. And if they continued to do as they pleased, that would not be tolerated any longer. They would have to be arrested and deported.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So let me just get the sequence of events right. There were Muslims held in the stadium. Through Pale, through contact with the authorities of Pale it's decided to bring these Muslims to Pale and, from there, they're removed out of the RS. After that, suddenly the paramilitaries are successfully removed. Right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: One group, the most extreme one and the worst one in Bratunac was removed, but the rest remained longer. The police tried in vain to cleanse Bratunac of those units and we were not successful in that, and as a result, we suffered consequences, both individually and generally, and all we encountered in Bratunac due to that were problems, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the interesting thing - I'll ask you about this - is that when Pale learned about this problem, they said, "Bring them here." They didn't say, "We'll send down help." They didn't say make sure those people were allowed to return to their homes. They didn't say, "We'll send units, MUP units, to help eject the paramilitaries." They said, "Bring them here," and then Pale ships them out of the RS territory; right? That's Pale's solution. Not to bring the Muslims home, to kick them out.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify this to you a bit, because I think that you are a little bit on the wrong course. These people had no place to go. Their families had gone to Tuzla. We didn't dare release them, because those others were against this, and unfortunately they enjoyed support of the part of the population. Therefore, we could not avoid any conflict with them, and we had no idea what the conflict would be. For that reason we charged Miroslav because this was beyond our local capacities and capabilities to seek assistance and help in any way whatsoever in order to solve this problem. We thought that it would be better for those people to be driven out of Bratunac quite safely and to be transferred to a territory where they would no longer suffer these problems. Now, how these conversations happened and what was discussed, I had never an opportunity to speak with Deronjic about this, but he did have some contacts at Pale, because I suppose he had to go to the highest level in order to seek solution. After that, we received permission for these people to be evacuated from the hall. We did that in the morning hours, because virtually overnight we prepared this plan, and we made sure that everybody was fully safe and secure, because that was really a terrible problem for everybody in Bratunac. Now, what happened between Miroslav and anyone at the top echelon, who he talked to and what he talked about, I don't know. I wasn't interested. After all, all I was interested was to have this problem solved because, as far as I'm concerned, I was only a member of the Crisis Staff and I was advocating a speedy release. And I said whatever solution is decided upon, they would have to leave because, in the first place, they hadn't come there of their own volition, and everything that was going on did not have any support from our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you were in your proofing session or when you met with Defence when you came here to The Hague --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise. Now, when you were in your proofing session when you came to The Hague and met with the Defence, whoever you met with, and met with Mr. Karadzic, did you discuss your meeting with Mr. Karadzic in Zvornik that took place in June 1992? Because it's not in your statement.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't. I have a clear recollection of this, and I have no difficulty in giving you all the details of it if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I'm asking you about - pay attention to my question - is whether you discussed this with the Defence and your answer was no. So nobody on the Defence side said, "Let's go through this meeting on -- that you had with me in Zvornik, with General Mladic, in June 1992." They just left that out.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they were supposed to be asking me about. I was at their disposal to speak about everything. I did say that we had that meeting and I did observe that it was noted down. It was shown to me in Mladic's report, a diary, whatever it was, that there was this part of mine, and as you read it, you can interpret it in different ways. And I'm prepared to say what is accurate and what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go to that now. So the answer is that the Defence did go through that meeting with you and show you that meeting, the notes in Mladic's notebook; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: In Mladic's notebook, yes, diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then it's nowhere in your statement, is it, that meeting or reference to it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I had -- I have never spoken about this meeting so far, officially. I did say that I remember it and that I'm prepared to explain it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll do that quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P01478, please. English 246, Serbian 245.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I know you keep good track of the time and probably you considered this, but it seems to me that the Prosecution has exhausted its time that you've allotted for cross-examination, and before you -- first of all, I think it's appropriate that, when they do so, they be the ones to ask you for additional time rather than to assume that the time will continue. So that's number one. Number two, while we don't normally oppose [indiscernible], we leave it to you whether the Prosecution should have extra time. I just want to point out that this is such a pattern when Mr. Nicholls examines witnesses who have 80 per cent of information about 1992 events in Bratunac in their statements and he spends 90 per cent of his cross-examination time on 1995 events in Srebrenica, only to get at the end to the material that's in the witness's statement or that deals with 1992. And we think that that's a pattern that ought to be addressed by limiting the amount of cross-examination time so that he, like every other member of the Prosecution team, fits his cross-examination into the allotted time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I respond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is for the Prosecution to decide how to cross-examine a witness. Could the court deputy approach the bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I take it you're coming to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I am coming to a close, Your Honour, but with your leave, I would like to respond to what Mr. Robinson has said and I think that's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First of all, it's absolutely none of his business how I conduct my cross-examination as long as my questions are not objectionable. Second of all, part of the pattern with the Bratunac witnesses he's referring to is for the Defence to file highly misleading, incomplete statements, as in with Jovan Nikolic, where they leave out that he attended -- that he learned about -- that he was at the Kravica warehouse on the 13th July. They just take that out of the statement and hope nobody's going to talk about it. These things take longer. I agree that I should request more time when I come to the end and I should try to stay within my limits. Second, by concentrating on some of these Srebrenica events, it goes directly to the credibility of the witness which covers his testimony and statement as a whole, and huge significant elements of what happens in Srebrenica are, as part of a pattern, left out of the Defence statements which is why they need to be dealt with longer on cross-examination. And we do -- I do not accept that Mr. Robinson is in a position to tutor me about how to cross-examine witnesses and I'll leave it at that. And I ask to have a little bit more time to conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please conclude in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, on the page we see in front of us, 246, in the English we see who was present, including you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to go now to page 249 in English, 248 in the B/C/S. Number 4, Branko Grujic from the interim government in Zvornik says: "We have 32.000 Serbs. We have successfully implemented the president's decision to settle Divic and Kozluk with our children." And I'm going to ask a question before I get an objection. Can we go to page 252 of the English and 251 of the B/C/S. Sorry, 253 of the English, 252 of the B/C/S. And this is Marko Pavlovic of the Zvornik command TO speaking, and he says: "We were most active in evicting the Muslims." And on the next page: "We had brought peace to Sepak, Divic, and Kozluk. Some of them wanted to move out while we demanded it. We had to evict some of the people also for the sake of our heroes who fled from Kovacevici."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now to you. Page 258 of the English. 257 of the Serbian. You are speaking and General Mladic writes: "Until 1968 it, Bratunac, had a Serbian majority population. Since then they've moved to Serbia. So according to the last census it was 64/36 in favour of the Muslims. In Bratunac municipality we now have two Muslims. We used to have paramilitary formations, today we have a clear situation ..." Now, I'm putting it to you, and you can answer this, that this is you reporting positively that Bratunac has been cleansed. The earlier statements by Grujic and Pavlovic, they are reporting the same thing more expressly, that they evicted the Muslims from Divic and Kozluk. You are then later reporting that you've done the same thing in Bratunac. That is the clear reading of this. You may now comment on my case to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Simic. Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This cannot wait the redirect. It would be proper for the witness to hear in the Serbian what is being read out, because the way Mr. Nicholls is presenting it is actually inaccurate, for instance, that Marko Pavlovic was talking about what it was that people wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I think the witness had the opportunity to read the relevant part of the notebook. Let's continue. Now can you answer the question, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Firstly, I don't know if this is only a portion of the notes taken at that meeting or the entire notes, but I do recall the meeting clearly. I will tell you how it was that I ended up there. Miroslav Deronjic was supposed to attend the meeting but he had to visit Kravica because there were some problems up there. He asked me to attend in his stead. He told me that there was going to be a meeting in Zvornik attended by somebody from the top and that I should bring along some information for the meeting. I didn't know what the nature of the meeting was, nor what sort of information I was supposed to bring along. I suppose it had to do with the strength of our army, how many there were, and what was going on. So I took it upon myself as personal task, I didn't have time to consult with him, to pay special attention to paramilitary units. And I was talking about the ratio of 64:32 -- 36, and I said that there were only -- the only Muslims that I was able to see as I was passing along the street are the two Muslim children. So what I did was I highlighted the fact that the miseries that we were experiencing in Bratunac were caused by the paramilitaries. In response to that, Karadzic cast a glance at Mladic who then held a small lecture on the issue of paramilitaries. I can give you a brief summary of that lecture that was intended for everyone. He said that for the most part these were people coming to those locations where there was copper, silver or gold. In other words, they would go there solely for plunder, for personal gain, and that they can only do damage to us. And my response to that was that we have satisfied ourselves of that, that it's quite clear to us, but that we simply don't have the strength to get rid of these people. We did that -- we tried that on a couple of occasions, we failed, and he promised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, the question was whether you reported this positively that Bratunac has been cleansed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This -- I put this ironically. I wanted to highlight the influence that the paramilitaries were wielding in Bratunac, and I wanted something to be done on this score. In response to that, Mladic, who must have caught my drift, promised to dispatch from Sekovici a unit of the military police. He said that there was a squad that was being trained for that purpose. I told him that the local military police and the local civilian police were unable to do anything. They would chase away a group of them. Our municipality is 60 kilometres away from the Drina, and then as soon as one group was chased away another would appear, across the river, on various boats or whatever, and this was a dead heat between us. We were trying to chase them away, and we were faced with the risk of death in the face of these individuals; whereas, on the other hand, the ordinary people grew mistrustful of us as we were unable to get rid of them. And then Mladic did act upon his promise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I think you answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask one more brief question? The witness has been giving long answers and I've been really trying not to cut him off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Popovic case here, you were cross-examined by the attorney for Colonel Beara about whether you could see the officer who you were later told was Colonel Beara when you met him in Bratunac on 12 July 1995, and this was your answer: "Q. Describe the officer that you claim you saw, sir. "A. I could easily describe him had I seen him clearly, but as we say, everything had -- all the blood had gone to my eyes." And then you say: "So at the time all I could see was the outline of the man and I saw that he was an officer." And you said: "I've already told you about my emotional state at the time and I have to admit I did not have any visual capabilities at all." You stand by that truthful testimony that you couldn't see the officer standing in front of you because the blood rushed to your eyes and you lost all your visual capabilities out of anger.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's not just the matter of being able to see. I was so irritated that I wasn't able to fully grasp what he was saying. I was asking that as a matter of urgency the people be evacuated from Bratunac before problems arise, and I was looking for somebody to evacuate these people from the stadium since with the passage of time their position grew ever more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So the answer's yes, you had no visual capabilities at all. You told the truth when you --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't know Beara as an officer. I don't know if it was him or not, and I said so at the time. I wasn't familiar with ranks to be able to tell what his rank was. Besides, I wasn't interested in that at all. At that point in time, I was only interested in finding somebody who would be able to release us of the trouble we had because what had been done was mindless to bring people over and keep them on buses overnight in the middle of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before Mr. Karadzic re-examines the witness, I think I should deal with this first. Can I draw the attention the parties to transcript page 45, line 21 to page 46, line 1. It's a transcript -- it's about the transcript from Bosnian court. I don't remember the case. Can we upload the 65 ter 24916, English page 22 and B/C/S page 23. Since only part of the passage was read to the -- to the witness, the meaning might have been different. The transcript reads -- our transcript reads: "Question from Defence counsel Krunic: And did you mention the incident when you were together with Deronjic, and you -- and what did he -- "Witness Simic: Yes, I found out that he had informed Radovan about what had happened." "That was truthful testimony, too, wasn't it?" And witness said yes. So it -- my question is related to what Deronjic allegedly reported to Karadzic, but the transcript from the Bosnian court has something more, so I'm going to read it out to the witness. So this is what you said in the Bosnian court. I'll read it out for you: "Yes. I found out that he," he meaning Deronjic, "he had informed Radovan about what had happened, whether he knows that it happened and that the army, according to him, acted irresponsibly by bringing people at all into the situation in which they found themselves." So, Mr. Simic, this is my question for you. Do you know what Deronjic reported to Mr. Karadzic at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I suppose he informed him of the event that happened at the Kravica farm co-operative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you heard that from Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the previous page, page 22 in Serbian of the document we have here. I don't know. Can we have the bottom of the page shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, a moment ago you said, and that was page 59, line 1: I suppose -- I believe he informed him. Have a look at what you said here. He probably heard about it later, and he probably sent word about it further. Which is true? Is what you said here true or what you said on page 59 true?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I assumed with quite a bit of certainty that Miroslav Deronjic had heard of -- about what had happened at Kravica and that it was his duty to inform you. This was something that you expected him to do. However, when I spoke about it with him, I can't recall at which point in time this was, I asked him, "Did you send word? Did you spread information?" He said that he did. What the time-frame was, we didn't discuss that. I didn't want to meddle into his duties. His duty was very responsible and I didn't want to interfere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The transcript did not reflect "probably." It seems that this word "probably" is eluding us. And you didn't -- you also said -- you didn't tell us who he informed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't tell me who it was who he informed. He only said he informed those up there. I didn't ask him who these people up there were. I supposed that he informed those whom he was supposed to inform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you know about the incident at Kravica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: As I said on a couple of occasions, I heard about the incident from Jovan Nikolic who, on the morning following the incident, came to my office to see the president of the Executive Board, Srbislav Davidovic, and there he told us how the event unfolded, what happened. He said that there were quite a few people killed up there and that it was the result of an incident caused by one of those who were rounding up these individuals who were part of that group and that what followed was random killing of the people probably as a result of fear, although I don't want to make a psychological analysis now of the minds of the people who were supposed to securing them over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the number of the persons killed that you learnt about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I never heard any numbers ever. Nobody spoke in terms of numbers. They only said that quite a -- that a lot of people had been killed there. What did that mean "a lot," I don't know, but nobody gave any figures. Nobody made count of the people. They just said that many people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the unit or formation deployed to Kravica to provide security there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I can't talk about it. I don't know. When Nikolic spoke about it, I wasn't interested in knowing who was securing them, which unit. My first response to that, of course, concerned the people in Kravica, who they were, and they told me that these people had probably been taken prisoner as they had been retreating as soldiers, and that they had been rounded up in a village beyond Kravica, and that somebody then ordered that these people be taken in. I suppose they were supposed to be transported. However, at that point, the incident took place resulting in the tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at your first answer here on the page in Serbian. Did this happen -- did he know that this happened and the army acted irresponsibly? Did you know or do you know now that it was the army that provided security there at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, this was to be expected. Who else would have been in charge of this military operation? In my belief, it would have been the army. And when I said that they made a mistake, I can explain what I meant, and my first response was that of a shock. How come these people ended up in Kravica? They were not supposed to be there to begin with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have pages 22 and 23 in Serbian admitted, as well as the corresponding English pages of the document we have in front of us. Can they be admitted as one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has no difficulty with it. Do you have any objection, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3400, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A round number. Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, do you know exactly what Deronjic allegedly told me about the incident at Kravica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he told you or if he spoke directly to you or to somebody else. I can say nothing specific about that. I suppose that he should have reported to you because you sent him there. There may have been an agreement between the two of you that he can give information to somebody else in case of your absence, but I never discussed his authority or his powers with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 55, line 8, the word "irony" didn't make it to the transcript. Judge Kwon asked you and then you clarified. And then you also said that you had said that the two Muslims were the Muslims in town, not the whole municipality, and even that was meant ironically; right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We only covered a small part of the area of some 10 to 15 square kilometres. The other territory belonged to villages bordering on other municipalities. There were barricades. We were unable to pass by there, and there were even some people killed in attempts to remove those barricades which stayed there until a military operation was launched. And those areas were strongholds from where attacks were carried out. That's how Kravica was hit, and both Serbian and Muslim villages were isolated or cut off from us and we were reduced to some 5 or 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Give me one moment, Your Honour. Okay. Page 62, lines 9 to 12. Mr. Karadzic said that the witness said: "And then you also said that you had said that the two Muslims were the Muslims in town, not the whole municipality." Could I have a cite to that, please? Maybe I'm missing it. I don't know what he's referring to. Maybe I missed it, in which case I apologise. I don't recall the witness saying that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 55, the transcript does not reflect what I said, that's why I intervened. Line 8. It was not reflected that all that had been said ironically. The percentage was 64 to 36 and that there were only two Muslims, but these two Muslims were the Muslims in town, not in the whole municipality. The transcript is wrong. We can check it against the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, then it's just a bit unusual that normally Mr. Karadzic make these transcript corrections at the time if there was something missing about municipality and Bratunac town instead of asking an incredibly leading question, putting it in. So I can check the tape, but I didn't see it in the transcript because it wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness mentioned seeing children passing along the street, and Mr. Karadzic pointed out there's some omission in the translation of the word "irony" or "ironic," so I take it that he meant to correct the transcript. Let's move on in any event.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. P1478, please. The page in Serbian is 251, and in English, 253. I believe these are the correct page numbers in e-court, or possibly 252 and 253. I'm referring to the typed version. 252. The following page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, the second paragraph from above, could you please read it out slowly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: "We had to move out a part of the people also because of our 'heroes' who fled from Kovacevici." But this is not our municipality, so I don't know whose words these are. Kovacevici, there is no such place in our municipality as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh. So move out --

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: "Part of the people also because of our heroes who fled from Kovacevici." Here obviously the word "heroes" is use ironically.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to draw your attention to those reading -- the attention of these reading the English version that the translation reads "evict," whereas a correct translation is "moved," because evict means forceful removal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could remind me whose words this is, Mr. Nicholls. Can we see the previous page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pavlovic, Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 24913. That's the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we're returning to 1992 and the issue of the evacuation of -- or, rather, while we're on this meeting at Zvornik, did I advocate ethnic cleansing at that meeting and what was my position with regard to the events that were unfolding in that sense?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I heard no word to that effect, and when it was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, because you overlapped with the interpretation, the interpreters had difficulty to understand you. Could you kindly repeat your answer, and please put a pause before starting answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear one sentence from you that could be interpreted as encouraging anything like that or supporting it, and when I spoke about the situation at Bratunac, you gave Mladic a long look, expecting obviously him to do something. That's how I understood it to mean. And I concluded that you had understood each other that a unit of reinforcement should be sent there, a unit from elsewhere, in order to resolve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether you were there at the time when Captain Dragan was at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: At this meeting we're discussing, I saw you and Mladic and some people who had been invited but nobody else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see page 4 of this document. Page 4 in the Serbian. I don't know about the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now let us try and shed some light on the following. It says here: "We from the Crisis Staff again reacted to this and demanded the political or police forces" -- just a minute. "Bearing in mind the situation as it was, we in the Crisis Staff decided to help those who had been imprisoned by supplying them with food and water. The president of the Crisis Staff informed the civilian and military authorities in Pale about the events and asked for a solution to the problems that had been created. I don't know at whose approval in any event it was obtained from Pale. We were given the assignment of transferring the captured men." That's what you said; right? Let's just see. It says here someplace that you supposed that Deronjic spoke to somebody.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is president of the Crisis Staff, and he was probably the only one who was able to do anything. The rest of us didn't know who to turn to, and at the time it was difficult to find anybody because the situation was chaotic everywhere more or less, and the institutions weren't -- or couldn't be reached at places where we would expect them. So Deronjic had to show initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at this document Mr. Karadzic read out. "Let's just see. It says here someplace that you suppose that Deronjic spoke to somebody." It says in the statement in English: "The president of the Crisis Staff informed the civilian and military authorities in Pale ..." So where is the "supposed," that he supposed that happened? It says it did happen in the statement. It's very leading to read out from the statement and then just ask for a yes, and it's even worse to change what's written in the statement and read it out as though it was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where is it, Mr. Nicholls? I have difficulty locating the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's on page -- top of page 5. Second sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There's no "supposed" in my translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is the passage Dr. Karadzic was reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Mr. Karadzic himself read that passage himself: "The president of the Crisis Staff informed the civilian and military authorities in Pale ..." Transcript page 65, lines 24, 25. Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but there is a sentence like: I suppose that Deronjic spoke to somebody. Whether it's in the minutes or this document I cannot tell now, but I can get around that. And besides, I got my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the dates, roughly, at least the period?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: This event happened, and I believe that it greatly contributed to the rampaging of these people in the town after the -- after deputy Goran Zekic was killed. The situation changed drastically. Both the Serbs and the Muslims believed that we would be able to preserve the peace on the next day started doubting everything and they didn't have a hope that anything good could be achieved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's nonresponsive, your answer. The question was about the date. If he's linking it to what happened with Mr. Zekic, that's fine, but it's still about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can try to assist you. Zekic was killed on the 8th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, but I've already said initially I'm bad when it comes to dates. Goran Zekic got killed before this event with the people in that hall. I'm positive. I was very near, and I sat with the man who was next to Goran Zekic who was -- he had blood all over him. Zekic drove, and this man was the -- sat in the passenger's seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it after the event at Glogova, and if so, how much later?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I think that just before Goran's death, we were informed the staff of Territorial Defence composed of reserve officers from Bratunac would go to Glogova to disarm them again because they knew from the previous instance that very few weapons had been handed in and that there would be more problems in the coming period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Try to be briefer, please. Do you remember when Glogova happened? And this incident, when it did happen, before or after Glogova?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: It was after Glogova. The first day after Glogova, Miroslav continued to collect weapons at Suha and somewhere else, and from Suha or wherever these people were brought in by the paramilitary units. They were taken to the gym at Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how long after they were brought were they sent to Pale?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, interpreters. Yes, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So shall I repeat what I said earlier? So Glogova --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. The question was how long after they were brought were -- they was -- were they sent to Pale.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it was three or four days later. I'm not quite sure. That would be more or less the time that they spent there, because we had to find someone. Miroslav was trying to find a solution to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's okay, but my question is: Do you recall when was the session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska held when I was appointed president?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that. We didn't have any communication signals and means at the time. We were not able to watch television, and we were not informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would the 12th of May ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I told you already that I have problems with the dates. However, if you mentioned an event, I can recall. When it comes to the dates, I'm not good at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 42, it wasn't recorded that there were only a few policemen. Can you concern -- confirm that you said that at that time there were only a few policemen in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the most striking shortage at that time in Bratunac was the lack of policemen. We have left with only a small number of professional police officers. There were also before that period only a few reserve police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's all right. It's all right. Now, this is the issue of transcript. Now, can you tell me where your house is located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: It's about a half an hour walking distance to the east. It's a suburb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 41, my learned friend Mr. Nicholls suggested to you that it was impossible that you hadn't seen the buses on the night between the 13th and the 14th of July, 1995. Is it possible to see the town from the village where you lived? If you say half an hour, that's about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear how many kilometres. Please could the speakers not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Did you mention, yourself, Mr. Karadzic, about distance?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, if the witness said half an hour, that would be 2.5 kilometres. I asked him to confirm whether it was half an hour walking distance and whether that coincides with the distance of 2.5 kilometres, because the witness says half an hour walking distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's leading. You should put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but we know that a person can cover 5 kilometres on foot. I just wanted to accelerate things, that was all. So I just wanted to ask him to translate half an hour of walking into a distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, about 2 kilometres, and everyone can check it because I still live where I had lived at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honours, to be clear, it may have been inadvertent, but I did not suggest that the witness could see the buses from his house. I was asking him if he was serious that he didn't see any buses because he was at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 31, the question contained an assertion that Mladic asked you to take food and water to the enclave. Were you supposed to take food and water to the enclave or to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: To Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 29, terrible discussions -- terrible conditions in Srebrenica were discussed. Can you tell me what was the population in the town itself during the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to Srebrenica or Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, Srebrenica, because the discussion was about horrible conditions in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know about Srebrenica. I suppose that about 10.000 people may have resided in the town itself. Srebrenica as a town is concentrated in an elongated shape and around a stream, and the houses there are pretty large. So I suppose that approximately it could accommodate about 10 .000 people, but I never paid attention to the statistical data either relating to Srebrenica or Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if 20- or 30.000 lived in Potocari and 13- to 15.000 fled to the forest, how many were living during the war in that same area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, there were more of them during the war than before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does it arise from the cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's also exceptionally leading - sorry to interrupt, Your Honour - to tell him if there were this many people here and this many people here and then you do the math I want, what do we arrive at. And the witness has already said he didn't know and he was speculating about the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we move on?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to find out how it derived because the suggestion was that these horrible conditions were imposed by the Serbs. I just wanted to hear how many people lived in the area that used to have 10.000 inhabitants and then had about 35.000 inhabitants during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic, but for planning purposes, how much longer do you need to conclude your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 10 and 15 minutes. Maybe it's better if we took a break, because I have some UN documents, contemporaneous UN documents to discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is 10 or 15 minutes, how about going long? I will ask the court deputy whether it is okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Try to conclude in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most certainly, Your Excellency. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked whether there was any mention of the evacuation while you were with Mladic, on page 13 you said nobody would have come to Srebrenica at this meeting in the brigade. How did you understand Mr. Nicholls' question that there was discussion with people from Srebrenica at 8.00?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, at 8.00 there were no Srebrenica representatives at the Bratunac Brigade, and I wasn't even aware of anyone having invited them to come to this meeting in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was any civilian from Srebrenica who were under the control of our authorities and army asked to return from Potocari to Srebrenica to their homes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, I didn't see such people. Maybe some of them stayed behind, but while I was walking with Mladic, I don't know what time it was, the Srebrenica streets were empty. I only saw two elderly people, a man and a woman, in the centre of the town, and they talked to journalists and Mladic joined them and conversed with them. That were the only people I saw moving around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were the foreigners, or, rather, representatives of the UN aware of what the Srebrenica civilians wanted with regard to their wish to either stay or go?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I do believe so, and I think that the huge majority of people of Srebrenica wished to leave the town due to the horrendous conditions because Srebrenica was overpopulated, because the population congregated there from all the other surrounding municipalities, and I can claim surely that Srebrenica had more inhabitants during the war than it had before the war. And even General Morillon mentioned that fact when I met him twice during his tenure and his engagement in Srebrenica. He knew that Muslims wanted to leave Srebrenica collectively, and he wanted to help them with that, and he managed to organise a convoy, whereas the other convoy was stopped by our army because pursuant to some earlier agreement some conditions were not met and, as a result, the convoy was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you recall, in which year did Morillon convey the wish of the Muslims to leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: It may have been 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please now see 1D3382 in e-court. This is a telegram sent by Ambassador Akashi to Annan and other persons for their information only. If you look at paragraph 2 at the bottom, and I'm going to read it out to you for interpretation: "[In English] Paragraph 5 should take account of the fact that, according to UNHCR, a great majority of the residents of Srebrenica do not wish to remain there. They are already displaced persons from elsewhere and will wish to move on."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does this fit to what you know about the wishes of the Muslims of Srebrenica and the knowledge that the international community had?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, this information is consistent with what they knew, and we all knew that some of them tried to run away towards Tuzla. And it is true that even before the outbreak of conflict a great many people left Srebrenica, which means that at the very beginning of all these dramatic events, Srebrenica was nearly an empty town. Goran Zekic and some young Muslims and Serbs were the only inhabitants initially.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3401, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 21087. It's a document of similar content admitted as a P exhibit but only one page. However, in this instance we have a document which is more complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the P number, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that would require some effort on my part to reorganise. I believe that was the last document shown by Mr. Nicholls as a P exhibit. It is a somewhat different format. The title is the same, but the format is different. Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Take a look at what it says in paragraph 4, and that is that the Medecins sans Frontieres had informed them that there were 10.000 people in Potocari inside the UN compound and 20.000 outside of it. And then they say that there were between 60 and 70 wounded people. And then paragraph 5 reads: "[In English] The plans of the UNHCR and UNPF conveyed yesterday in my Z-1139 to evacuate all those people from Srebrenica wishing to leave have encountered at least initial resistance from the Bosnian government authorities. As indicated, the UNHCR SE will be meeting with Bosnian minister for refugees Cero in Tuzla today, at which meeting satisfactory agreement and arrangements can hopefully be worked out." [Interpretation] And somewhat down below: "[In English] Bosnian minister Mulatovic made the following points: "(a) Local Bosnian officials in Srebrenica are not authorised to negotiate on behalf of the Bosnian government at least until proper communications can be established with them; and (b) the Bosnian government does not accept the movement of any people out of the enclave other than in the case of medical emergency; (c) Srebrenica is a UN safe area and the newly displaced should be accommodated there; (d) adequate accommodation for a large influx of displaced is not available in Tuzla which is already saturated with displaced persons," and so on. [Interpretation] Was it known was that the central Bosnian government in Sarajevo was resisting the evacuation of civilians regardless of what their wishes were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, it was this first attempt made by Mr. Morillon. I don't know with whom. I didn't have any information about it. It was for the most part carried out by the army and Morillon. Evidently, they wanted to prevent this. They did not meet one of the basic criteria, as Morillon put it, that some of the Bosnian Serbs from Tuzla be evacuated on the journey back. Apparently Morillon said that Alija Izetbegovic had tricked him, that he had promised him this, and that when this first convoy went out, it was supposed to bring Serbs as well. But on the second convoy, he went back on this promise and then our people no longer allowed other convoys to take place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it -- yes, I have the information. The second document in this 65 ter number, i.e., page 4 and 5, were admitted as separate number, Exhibit P3974. So there's no need to admit it separately. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just say if Mr. Karadzic wanted to ask this witness about this document, the witness can't read the document and about what it shows about who wanted to leave and why and who would not accept that, then he should have read paragraphs 2 and 3 of page 1. The witness could understand what was -- the preamble to this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us leave it. I forgot to mention this was admitted as Exhibit P5197.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But only the first page; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Three pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it was not correctly noted in e-court. Can we have 65 ter 16851 for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this, Mr. Simic, can you tell us the approximate time of arrival of that convoy?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: The one that was taken out by Morillon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. The 12th. The time of arrival of the convoy. You said that you were told that it was going to arrive in the evening.

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: At sunset. I don't wear a wristwatch, so that's how I recall that it arrived just before the sun set.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long would they have been on the 12th of July in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, it was summertime. I didn't pay much attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in this document that was drafted at 6.00 and arrived at 7.19, it's dated the 12th of July and says that Srebrenica fell and that the evacuation was nearly over. And then on page 3 -- I'm sorry, on page 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm trying to keep up. He's reading from page 1 just now. Where does it say the evacuation is nearly over? Are you talking about paragraph 1 which says it's just commenced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give it a look now. I was rushing a bit. Yes, right. The evacuation has commenced. But the document was supplemented in the course of the day, and there are supplements as separate documents as well. However, this final document produced at 6.00 has all the supplementary information. You have the update on page 2, and then another update and yet another. So it's a collection of reports, and in one of these updates it is stated that it is nearly complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But Mr. Nicholls is correct. You need to cite very accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think a document from the 12th can be updated to say the evacuation is nearly complete, and I don't see it in here although I haven't had a chance to read the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you need a break, we'll break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll finish with this document, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at page 4, item 3, that the supply of water has not been cut off and that there is food for two meals only until the 13th for all the people who are there. At page 5 there is mention of, under point 2: "[In English] The situation now remains calm but tense. The commanding officer of DutchBat is again holding a meeting accompanied by a selected few of the refugees and with the BSA to negotiate for humanitarian aid from the BSA. Info received indicates that BSA have accepted to assist with food and water. UNMOs and MSF are, however, further negotiating for medical assistance." [Interpretation] Did you know that Mladic and the army promised and did help with the delivery of water and food supplies?

utterances.speaker: LJUBISAV SIMIC
utterances.text: I arrived there in Potocari later. It was probably finished by that time I took up the duties I came there for. As for medical care it was working in proper order. Those injured were transferred to the health centre in Bratunac and we also had an ambulance there with medical staff in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The beginning questions in the premise of showing this document was about the time the convoy arrived on the 12th. That's how Mr. Karadzic started this line of questions using this document. Is he saying this document says that a convoy arrived on the 12th from UNHCR of food?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, if this report was completed by 6.00, then everything that followed after 6.00 would not have been contained in this report but in the report issued on the following day, the 13th. That was the point I was trying to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, but just trying to keep the record semi-straight and honest, the reports of the 13th say that the convoy arrived in the evening after all the refugees had left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's leave it at that. It's the subject of your further submission. Let's get on with the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted? But in essence it isn't that important because -- well, the witness said that he wasn't that good handling the various dates. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3402, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Simic. Thank you, Excellencies. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless my colleagues have a question for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Simic. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. We'll rise all together. We will have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There certain change of members. Good afternoon, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, I'd like to address the Chamber on a matter related to, in fact identical to, the matter I rose before you on yesterday, and that's with regard to the late notification of material. So yesterday, if I do have leave, I addressed Your Honours about the late notification of General Galic's expected evidence in chief and documents which included untranslated material, and even after that, raising that with Your Honours, last night after the examination-in-chief of General Galic had already begun, the Prosecution was or the parties were notified of a further additional 28 documents that Dr. Karadzic wished to use with General Galic in his examination-in-chief, and seven of those are untranslated. So, Your Honours, because of my having risen yesterday and because the exact thing I complained about yesterday has effectively -- has continued, I felt compelled to rise and make further submissions. We are, under heading 2(g) of Your Honours' guidelines for the conduct of trial, required a file a final list of documents or material that might be used during the examination-in-chief of a witness no later than 48 hours before that examination-in-chief begins. And there have been cases, I recall some personally and there may be some that arose with my other colleagues, there have been cases, small in number, where the Prosecution has accepted additional documents while the examination-in-chief was underway. But the circumstances in this case given the lateness, given the nature of the material that was disclosed on Saturday, given the volume of the material that has disclosed last night, and that in light of my concerns yesterday I'd say the circumstances in this case now are extreme, and I would like to submit something to Your Honours for consideration. Under heading 2(g) of Your Honours' guidelines which deals with disclosure of material which is going to be used in cross-examination, a party seeking to use a document or material during cross-examination that was not listed or disclosed according to the provisions of that section may be permitted to use that material on showing good cause, and because of the situation that's arisen and the number of documents we received last night in blatant, I would submit, disregard of Your Honours' guidelines, I would submit Your Honours might find it appropriate to require Dr. Karadzic to show cause similarly for each and every late document he now wishes to add. And furthermore, Your Honours, just with respect to the untranslated material that we received both Saturday night and last night, I would request in these circumstances that Dr. Karadzic should not be entitled to use these documents with the witness until they're translated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Well, first of all, our principle remains the same that we agree that the Prosecution should be allowed to have as much time as they need before having to cross-examine the witness and if as a result of these materials being disclosed to them at the time they were they need more time, we don't oppose that. We have good cause, actually, for not having disclosed these materials earlier, because what happened was when General Galic came to the Detention Unit last week for the first time, which was the first time we were able to have any contact with him, he was proofed by Mr. Sladojevic and it wasn't until Saturday that Dr. Karadzic first encountered General Galic and was able to have his own proofing session. And after that session, when the proofing note was prepared and he saw what the topics were, he realised that something that had been left out was documentation that supported General Galic's testimony about the scheduled incidents, and so he directed our team to -- he gave us some documents and directed us to include those in the documents being uploaded to e-court and disclosed to the Prosecution for use during the testimony of General Galic, and that's exactly what we did and we did it as soon as we could. So that's the actual factual situation as to why this last group of documents came when it did. So we propose to use those documents with General Galic. To the extent that they're not translated, like other documents used with Rule 92 ter witnesses that are untranslated, they can be discussed in court and marked for identification, and if the Prosecution needs more time before cross-examining on those documents, either the language section or their own services can translate them so that the Prosecution's cross-examination can proceed. But anyway, we were working under conditions that are somewhat unusual with this witness because of our lack of access to him, and we've done the best we could under the circumstances. But the bottom line is that there's no grounds or precedent for prohibiting us or excluding these documents since, as we know, the Prosecution on at least 62 occasions has been found to have failed to disclose to us documents which we might have otherwise wanted to use, and there 's never been any remedy of exclusion for those disclosure violations, and it would be unfair to begin imposing a remedy like that on the Defence at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were those documents additionally added on the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Most of them I don't believe were on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Under the circumstances, having heard Mr. Robinson's submission, the Chamber finds there's a good cause on the part of the Defence, and we'll allow them to be used, and if necessary, the Chamber is minded to allow a short adjournment to the Prosecution upon request. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon. From what I understood, Witness Galic has a technical problem. He can't access the transcript, which he should be able to follow in order not to speak too fast. It seems that he can't see the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for informing that to us. Probably inadvertently pushed a button. Do you see the transcript, General, now? Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General, sir. Good afternoon, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, yesterday we started discussing the topic of outgoing fire, provocation, and attacks. In that period of time in 1993, was there any change in the intensity of fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke of the enemy fire, the BH Army fire. In 1993, I believe that the pace or intensity remained the same or similar. It didn't change much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did your view that you should not return fire unless strictly necessary change?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this position was taken on all of our levels with a view to honouring the agreement and to reducing our losses. Whenever we were not strictly forced to return fire, we did not do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 1D01473.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may have rushed a bit. I haven't finished my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The response to fire would follow after we sustained losses. I'm sorry, I was waiting for the transcript to run, and you have rushed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness said that there would be response to fire after losses were sustained or after an attack commenced. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we sustained serious losses, that's what I said, or after an attack was mounted which would threaten our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All units? The General has been speaking slowly, but we haven't had everything reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure the pace will be better later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be of assistance to everyone, I confirm that the problem stems from the English translation, and the French translation keeps abreast of the pace so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 1D01473. We've been waiting for it for a while now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is dated the 4th of February, 1993, the situation as at 1800 hours. You see it says here that the attack commenced at 1700 hours with 120-millimetre shells targeting Nedzarici from the direction of Dobrinja 5 and the Olympic village, that such a combined artillery and infantry attack was still ongoing and there was sniper fire. You said that you were at the lines reached and that your focusing on reconnaissance and observation of enemy activity. What does this mean that you're not returning fire yet but you are only observing and reconnoitering?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I go back to that period of time of the 4th of February, 1993, I'm sure there must have been specific reasons why we did not respond to this sort of threat in terms of fire and risk to which our territory was exposed. I suppose that there was a specific reason why we did not want to return fire at once. I suppose that in the meantime a protest was lodged with UNPROFOR that the BH Army should desist from further attacking our lines or else we would return fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said earlier on whenever there were serious losses. Here we have one soldier wounded and one child wounded as well, and this wasn't sufficient for you to return fire; right?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell Their Honours here that I regretted every death we had during the war, and the situation in Sarajevo was particularly difficult, the Sarajevo front line, and I was especially aggrieved by the death of children. And it's -- I'm not the sort of person who would say one thing and do another, and I felt particularly sorry for children. And thus, in this case, we had a child that -- who died, but probably the decision at the time was that we should not place at risk our greater goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what the sentiments were on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are not to comment and the last part of previous question was also leading. You have to ask this witness whether this document is saying whether VRS was firing or not. Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. I was rising about the leading question before we moved on further. But only a caution, because I see it already and hear it already, for Dr. Karadzic who has experience in this courtroom to wait until the translation is completed so that we can all hear what's going on accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So while we have this document before us, Mr. Galic, it's not clear from this document whether the SRK was returning fire or not because it does not say anything about it except saying it was observing with the aim of monitoring enemy activity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're going to ask the General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I asked the question to Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As for the earlier comments from the Chamber and the Prosecution, I accept them and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I'd like to ask you this: Why does it not say here whether you returned fire or not?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not written here because -- well, this was signed by my chief but let me answer your question nevertheless. It is not written here for the following reason. Whatever we returned fire, we would record exactly which were the areas that we responded to. There was once when I was speaking about artillery and other combat assets when I said that we always had to note down whatever was used to respond, whatever assets we used, it had to be noted down. So in this case the situation was that we did not return fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3402, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D01478, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll follow up on your previous reply once we see what this document says. It says here between 1600 and 1630 hours, that is, half an hour, ten shells hit our positions. And in item 2 your units are mentioned, and it says the artillery of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade replied to enemy action from Mojmilo and Dobrinja 3 in order to neutralise it and protect their units. Can you explain what this means.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our estimate at the time that given the use of enemy units and their activities, these areas and units were threatened and that we had to return fire and neutralise the source of enemy fire. We targeted those areas from where enemy fire came, I see here. I also have to read it first to be sure that this is the case. This is from my corps command and was sent to the Main Staff. But yes, this is what we spoke about yesterday and are still discussing today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And here it says: After 1700 hours, our forces did not open infantry or artillery fire and were in the zone. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at item 1, the time period is from 1600 to 1630. That is the time of enemy activity. After a certain time we responded and that is roughly the time artillery needs to respond, about a quarter hour. Irrespective of the types of artillery fire that exist. And after half an hour -- or, rather, within half an hour there was no response from our side. It's good that this was drafted this way, because it reflects the rhythm, and this is how combat tasks were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would have happened, General, if you had not responded by targeting these firing positions? What would the enemy have done on that day?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It calls for speculation I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. The General can speak from experience. I'm sure he knows what happens unless you show your teeth, unless you respond.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you don't respond, they mostly continue their activity against our forces. They always look for means and ways to inflict losses on us and move the front line. We saw that yesterday on that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Galic, could you read the second sentence in paragraph 2, starting from: "The 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The artillery of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade responded to enemy action from Mojmilo and Dobrinja 3 in order to neutralise it and protect their own units. I believe that's what we said. I explained why the response was like this and in which areas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is: If you read the next sentence it expresses SRK as "our units," but I was wondering what "their units" were? To protect their own units. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as for item 2, that was the style these reports were drafted. Under 1, you report about the enemy; under 2, you report about your own forces; under 3, you describe the situation in the territory. This is a perfect example of the way all reports are drafted. Our units -- it always reads the combat readiness of the SRK units, the corps units. And such a report can also include a decision about the activities to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, I see what the problem is. It reads "their units" but it should read "our units." It was translated as "their own units" again. It's incredible that "our units" are translated as "their units" or maybe the interpreter simply read the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. It's noted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before we do that, this is the second document that the General has commented on today that's not signed by him. The first one he indicated was signed by his chief. And with respect, we know nothing about his chief, why his chief would sign the documents and he not, or the circumstances in which his chief would sign these documents, whether he or not he indeed saw them if his chief would sign them. And I would think that that would be the sort of foundational questions or foundational evidence we would -- should hear before admitting this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that could be taken up in your cross-examination but let's hear from the witness. Can you assist us, Mr. Galic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reports are mostly drafted by the staff. When I'm present and not busy otherwise, I read the report, but when it's taken elsewhere to be amended or encoded, sometimes it is simply signed by the Chief of Staff or the officer standing in for me. That's a report of the command, it's not a personal report, so that the whole command stands behind this report. Each morning and each evening there was the briefing. We summarised our reports and analysed them. It was impossible for anything to be sent out to inform the Main Staff by chance or arbitrarily. But I as a commander stand by all such reports although this was signed by my chief, but he's my deputy so he has the authority to sign documents for me and he had the right to certify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3403, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see 1D01480.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated two days later, General. Can you please tell us what the enemy was doing? Item 1 refers to the enemy. Artillery fire on Ilidza, the barracks Grbavica, one civilian killed, four wounded. What were the -- the usual losses per day? Is this an ordinary, average day or is this an exception?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During a war all days are the same or very similar. It all depends on what happened and what orders were issued to one side or the other.
