Were orders issued about limiting activities or launch activities or to ban offensive activities, and the goal's always the same, the goals of the warring parties. This is a normal war day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Item 2 says that the corps units responded adequately to enemy fire. Could you please explain what that means, "adequately"?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This term "adequately" is widely used in military vocabulary. It was used often during the war. It means that when there was a fire from infantry weapons, then the response would also be from infantry weapons. During my trial there was always the problem with distinguishing between infantry fire and sniper fire. It was alleged that it was the same, but it's not. So when there was infantry fire, you respond by firing from infantry weapons. When there was mortar fire, you respond with your own mortars. We did not have recoilless guns -- or, actually, we did but we didn't have ammunition, so I don't think the entire corps during my command fired a single shell from a recoilless gun, whereas they used to extensively. I could tell you stories about that, but there's no time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us about item 4. It says: Weariness and psychological strain. What were the shifts on the front line in the SRK, and what was it like in the 1st Corps of the BH Army with regard to numbers or manpower?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This is the core of the problem of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. We didn't have depth of territory to man our forces. We didn't have enough forces to have some soldiers in reserve. We were drawn out along the front line like a web only to cover the 65 kilometres that we mentioned yesterday because we had too few soldiers and too few units. Unit rotation was supposed to happen once a week. However, in reality, only the 2nd Romanija Brigade was able to do so, whereas others were -- spent their time on the front line and half their time at home. That's why the fighters were weary. This was February 1993, so it's winter, and that's another reason why the soldiers were weary and tired and that must be mentioned. If we look at the manpower we had at our disposal, our side and theirs, we will see that at the Sarajevo front we had about 10.000 men. I'm referring to only that area. Whereas the 1st Corps of the BH Army on average had 35.000. We supposed that they were even more numerous during certain periods, even up to 40.000 or so. What were their resources like in terms of manpower to cover all axes? We saw that their brigades are deployed battalion by battalion, whereas we were unable to do that because we had pull people out for them to rest. So they were able to rest longer and rest almost entire units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were talking about 35- to 45.000 soldiers. Are you talking about forces in the city itself or do you include those at the Nisic plateau, at Hadzici and on Mount Igman. Later, those were the 14th and 16th Divisions. Who are you talking about when you say 35- to 45.000?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the forces that were mostly in Sarajevo, the 1st Corps, and I spoke about the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps which are linked with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat and speak a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said you were speaking about the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the part of it that was oriented toward Sarajevo. And what are you talking about when you speak about the 1st Corps of the BH Army and their 35.000 to 45.000 men? Which forces are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to -- I have to go slow. I'm referring to the forces of the 1st Corps of the BH Army that were in Sarajevo. And I must add to that, because I spoke about this Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, I must also describe the situation in the 1st Corps of the BH Army. As far as we knew, in 1992, 1993, the 1st Corps of the BH Army had about 78.000 soldiers, 78.000. The Prosecutor admitted as much during my trial as well. If we add to that the reinforcements up there and you mentioned them in connection with Ilijas or in the Olovo area, those are the forces of the 3rd Corps that later became an operative group, Visoko and Vares. But I don't know when divisions were formed because I had already gone. These are not included in the numbers I mentioned. These 78.000 [Realtime transcript read in error "38.000"] were in Sarajevo on Mount Igman and they were holding the territory up to the Drina area and Gorazde, and the 1st Corps covered all that territory. And that's what their zone was according to our estimates. So much about these forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 7 it should read "78.000" instead of "38.000" because that's what the witness said, 78.000. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 78.000.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3404, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D10505 [as interpreted], please. 01505. 1D01505.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated 15th of March. Let's not talk about the sniping mentioned in paragraph 4, but in item 2, you say that our forces managed to repel the attack and then you speak about unexpected events, that is to say, that they fired from Butmir at Igman. Four shells fell. One soldier was killed, and 14 detainees were wounded. And you say that all these detainees were Serbs. Did our enemies know what the Kula prison was and who was kept there?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the people living in Sarajevo knew what the Kula prison was. We know that the majority of our troops were originally from Sarajevo and that applied to the 1st Corps of the BH Army as well. Their people were from Sarajevo, even though I must say that they had more people from outside of Sarajevo. So the command knew what was in this prison in Kula, and that there were detainees held there who had no weapons, who were only serving their sentences there and were doing only jobs according to the plans made by the prison administration. Now, forgive me for being so blunt but I must say that a driver was -- my driver was injured. I put him in detention because he did something that he was not supposed to do. So we had to treat everyone equally, but it seems that here only Serbs were wounded. I don't know how many Muslims were incarcerated there, because this prison was run by the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And here it says that an UNMO came to establish whether there was there was a violation of cease-fire. Did that happen during cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most definitely since this is what is noted here, and I think that UNPROFOR also lodged some protest requesting that such facilities not be targeted. But I don't think that this facility specifically was often targeted as other facilities were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3405, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D01509. We're going to skip some dates, but if the Chamber think it is appropriate, we're going to look at each daily report according to bar table which will show exactly how things developed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this regular combat report dated the 18th of March, where you say that several hundred shells fell on Ilidza. And then you go on to say, under item 2, that the Ilidza, the Rajlovac and the Vogosca brigades were actively involved in operations according to plan. Can you tell the Chamber what did you mean by carrying out active operations according to plan?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can see here, because when something like this is being said, that obviously relies to the previous report which clearly says what the plan was. As I can see, this is 18th of March, 1993, and that the Vogosca, Rajlovac and Ilidza brigades were engaged in combat. They did take part in the activities towards the Nisic plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you speak about the consumption and the active operations, did you present summary consumption on the inner circle or outer circle or are these two figures presented separately?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A summary report made by a corps is always made as a whole. It doesn't make a distinction between the inner ring or the outer ring. The Igman Brigade, which was deployed both to Sarajevo and Ormanj, it showed its total losses incurred on that day. For example, if a number of grenades fell which caused certain losses, they would present their total losses, but they would indicate specifically what they did and that is the basis for everyone to understand what they did and why they suffered such losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3406, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D01514, 1D01514.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is 22nd March 1993. This report reads that about 200 shells hit Ilidza and resulted in the death and injuries of civilians. What was so militarily attractive in Ilidza? Was there any military installation in the civilian part of Ilidza to warrant such an enormous number of shells being fired on it?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the very centre of Ilidza there was nothing apart from the municipal building and you know exactly how Ilidza looks like, but towards the source of the Bosna River was the brigade's command post. Perhaps that was their target. Anyway, if you go beyond towards the -- in depth of Ilidza, there was nothing that was militarily interesting. That was the place where the civilian facilities were only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the source of the Bosna. Was there any waterworks there and do you know anything -- do you know whether these shells caused damage to this installation and transformer stations?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which particular report speaks about this but I do know that for a period of time a transformer station in Hadzici was a target. So that is part of the electrical grid and it goes from Hadzici to Ilidza and Sarajevo. And if electricity is cut off, that means that there is no water supply as well. We had some water sources there, and one particular source was called Bacevo, which is located more towards Stojicevac. Do you want me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. All I wanted to ask you, whether when they were firing on Ilidza -- probably the answer can be found under item 3, where it says in the report that the security of citizens has been violated due to intense enemy artillery against populated areas. Where was the origin of this fire that targeted the populated area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I find, in my submission, that Dr. Karadzic is starting to be quite leading in the way he is asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not putting questions to the witness. All I'm doing is reading the document and it says that there were wounded and killed civilians in Ilidza, and all I'm asking is about the origin of fire. We can see where the shells landed but where did they come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, having discussed with the witness about the ways in which the VRS responded to various attacks, the Chamber sees no difficulty with the accused going through the combat report which the witness himself wrote. Unless there's some special circumstances in which he needs to put some foundational cases, the Chamber will allow the accused to carry on. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So let me simplify things. My first question was: Was there fire targeting populated area their response to fire coming from our positions?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you read in the report from which direction it came, it came from Donji Kotorac and other positions in Vojkovici, which is an area more to the east. That means that from our populated area there was no fire opened. For example, we had our positions outside of Ilidza. We didn't have any deployment inside the town itself. Maybe a command post or something similar to that, and that's what the BH Army had as well in their part. As for the deployment of our artillery and other weaponry, we always tried to deploy military units in the vicinity of populated area as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Outside the populated areas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both their side and our side found this to do difficult and found it almost impossible to -- not to deploy or have a piece of weaponry that would be a legitimate target if it is positioned close to a civilian facility. That was the essence of it. We did our best, but let's be honest, it wasn't always possible to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3407, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can now have 1D01521, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is already the 5th of April. Sir, this is at 1400 hours, and it says at around 10.00 in the evening, on the 4th April, ten shells fell on Grbavica and two shells hit Kaponiri, at the old airport. They fired from a Browning and one house was set on fire. Now, under item 2, our forces, it says as follows: Our forces are honouring truce along the -- reached our lines and very seldom opened fire from infantry weapons at the observed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you -- no, just a second. Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked the witness to tell the Chamber why there was no response or why they responded only rarely, and to describe how the two warring parties behaved themselves on this specific day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before you answer the question, Mr. Galic, can I ask you to read out bullet point 2, para 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Para 2. "Our forces are at the lines reached and are observing the cease-fire and only rarely upon approval opened fire from infantry weapons upon observed targets."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see a slight difference in English translation. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In item 7 and onwards, an UNPROFOR convoy was stopped or perhaps it was a UNHCR convoy. Or rather, yes, can you answer my question about why it was that you returned fire only rarely. In item 2 you say that fire was opened rarely.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we look at all the various assets that we used to fire upon our forces, we will see that a response from infantry weapons was not an appropriate or adequate response, so we reduced it to what would be an adequate response. And then, as I can see, a cease-fire was still in force and the use of all assets was banned. So why was it decided to open fire only selectively? Well, in order to neutralise the enemy in a way or to simply make him refrain from opening fire which was observed under para 1 here, and that was why this sort of response as described here was chosen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was another question that you put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's a separate topic.

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It should be marked MFI, then, as this is a Defence uploaded document so that they can request a revised translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think we're happy to request the revised translation, but I think it's been our practice to admit the translated documents even though there may be revisions required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, with that caveat, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3408, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, the Defence is tempted to seek adequate resources to ask for all the translations to be revised, because the translations are so poor as to change the meaning of the text. And we will be seeking your support in this request unless we find the Registry to be accommodating in this respect. Can we now call up 1D01525.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: While that's coming up, I should probably note that that translation error was actually in our favour, so sometimes errors can go both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this is already May. We are therefore skipping a couple of weeks here. So we see that the enemy fired on the general area of the north-western part of the front, on urban areas and industrial plants, and it says that attacks were successfully repelled. Can we have the next page. There is a surprising issue here, and you can tell us what this is all about, under D, forecast or outlook, where it says: Today, at around 10.30, the enemy engaged own forces by targeting the BH Presidency and the Ukrainian Battalion command. They are trying to make their own combat activities appear as those of the VRS and have lodged protests with UNPROFOR representatives and the mass media. What are your comments on this?

utterances.speaker: STANISLAV GALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, having looked at this report, I think the matter is quite clear. The Presidency is being targeted, which is a civilian feature, although, of course, it has grown into a Supreme Command, as it were. Though we refrained from firing upon the Presidency. Now, next, fire upon UNPROFOR members, members of the Ukrainian battalion. I don't know when exactly it happened that the Ukrainian Battalion member was hit by the BH Army. Was it on that same day? I'm not sure, it may have been the case, but I know that later on it was said that a member of the Ukrainian Battalion was killed. Fire of this sort most certainly damaged our side, because it was being insinuated that and attributed to our side. Whenever there was fire upon the Presidency, who would be to blame? Well, everybody would say that it was the SRK forces rather than the forces of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. Or if you adjust the various angles as the Sevas did or I don't know who else in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps of the BH Army in Sarajevo, they even had their own pathologists who would adjust the data so as to make it appear as if the origin of fire was from the SRK. So it was difficult to prove that the SRK forces were not to blame. That's why we were reporting such events to the Main Staff. And it doesn't say here but I do assume that a protest or a warning of some sort, an alert, was submitted to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be an admitted. I note the time. We're waiting for the Chamber's ruling on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3409, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for today. We need to give some time to prepare for Mr. Tieger and Mr. Robinson for tomorrow. Mr. Galic, there will be no trial hearing tomorrow and we'll continue on Thursday. I take it you understand that you're not supposed to discuss about your testimony with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not really discussing it anyway. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.
